expectations.text: Output flags that the 'same items for everyone therefore items are fixed' reasoning is incorrect
expectations.evidence: The model devotes a full section to 'The "but my images are fixed/selected" objection' and explicitly states: 'The argument "images aren't random, so no random effect" conflates two different questions.' It directly dismantles the reasoning the user presented.

expectations.text: Output explains that items should be treated as random because the researcher wants to generalize beyond these specific 48 images to the population of similar stimuli — which requires treating items as a random sample
expectations.evidence: 'And you almost certainly want the condition effect to generalize beyond exactly these 48 images. Without (1 | image), you're not testing that.' The generalization argument is clearly and directly made.

expectations.text: Output recommends adding by-item random effects — (1 | item) at minimum, and by-item random slopes for within-item conditions if applicable
expectations.evidence: The model recommends the minimum model as `lmer(rating ~ condition + (1 | subject) + (1 | image))` and also presents a maximal model with `(condition | image)` for when condition varies within images: 'Start maximal and simplify only if you hit convergence problems.'

expectations.text: Output does NOT validate the advisor's framing or agree that fixed-item analysis is appropriate
expectations.evidence: While the model agrees the subject random intercept is necessary, it explicitly corrects the advisor's overall framing: 'your advisor's reasoning needs one more step' and 'The single random intercept your advisor approved is a common starting point but misses half the crossed structure.' The fixed-item approach is never endorsed.

expectations.text: Output references Clark (1973) / language-as-fixed-effect fallacy, OR Judd et al., OR explains that treating items as fixed means conclusions don't generalize beyond those 48 specific images
expectations.evidence: The model explicitly names both: 'This is Clark's (1973) "language-as-fixed-effect fallacy" generalized to visual stimuli, and it's directly addressed by Judd, Westfall & Kenny (2012).'
